name: Huberman sleep stack

lead: The Huberman sleep stack is a bedtime combination of magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine, linked to neuroscientist and podcaster Andrew Huberman. People use it to sleep better, which appearance communities treat as a foundation for skin, energy and looks.
Each ingredient is proposed to calm the nervous system by a different route. No published trial of the three-ingredient combination was found, and each ingredient has limited human sleep data.

paras: The three supplements are taken together in the evening before bed, usually as capsules or powder, and people judge it by sleep quality over days to weeks.
The ingredients are sold as supplements, which are loosely regulated, so quality varies. Critics of Huberman's supplement promotion say the claims go beyond what research shows.

angle.text: Popularized by a podcaster, this bedtime trio is used to improve sleep, which appearance communities treat as a foundation for skin, energy and a rested look. The combination has not been tested as a unit.

lead: The Huberman sleep stack is a bedtime supplement combination, commonly described as magnesium threonate, apigenin and theanine, associated with Stanford neuroscientist and podcaster Andrew Huberman. People take it to fall asleep more easily and sleep more deeply, and appearance communities often treat good sleep as a foundation for skin quality, energy, training recovery and overall looks.

Andrew Huberman, an associate professor of neurobiology and ophthalmology at Stanford, launched the Huberman Lab podcast in 2021 and has published the book Protocols.[1] Wikipedia reports that he has promoted dietary supplements, which commentators such as Jonathan Jarry have criticized as poorly regulated.[1] Wikipedia's article on him does not discuss the stack itself.

Each component is sold separately: magnesium L-threonate is a magnesium salt reported to reach the brain more readily than ordinary magnesium,[2] apigenin is a plant flavone that is most abundant in chamomile flowers, parsley and celery,[3] and L-theanine is an amino acid from tea.[4] No published trial of the three-ingredient combination as a unit was found.

paras: The stack is taken in the evening. Its components are individually sold as supplements. Apigenin is a plant flavone and in chamomile flowers makes up about two thirds of the flavonoids; in laboratory work it binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors, though researchers disagree about how it interacts with that site, and human trial data for sleep are not described in encyclopedic sources.[3] Theanine was discovered in green tea in 1949 and makes up roughly 1 to 2 percent of green tea leaf dry weight.[4] See the separate entries on magnesium threonate and on chamomile and passionflower tea for more on those ingredients.

sections.h: What research says about the components
paras: The European Food Safety Authority found in 2011 insufficient evidence that theanine helps maintain normal sleep, a 2020 review suggested theanine might reduce stress and anxiety in people experiencing acute stress, and a 2025 review judged the research inconsistent and weak.[4] The US FDA treats theanine as generally recognized as safe in foods and drinks at up to 250 mg per serving.[4]
For magnesium L-threonate, Wikipedia cites one small placebo-controlled trial in healthy Chinese adults on cognition, published in Nutrients in 2022, and says nothing about sleep.[2]

Critics cited by Wikipedia say Huberman's podcast sometimes presents certainty where evidence is ambiguous and applies animal research to humans without adequate justification; New York Magazine said he often posits certainty where there is ambiguity.[1] Supporters regard his protocols as accessible summaries of neuroscience. The podcast has been sponsored by companies whose products critics consider questionable, and neuroscientist David Berson has noted that peers did not always approve of the monetization.[1]
No studies found of the combination.
